say.text: A state health team must name the one cancer that leads its women's screening drive, using current registry figures.
Which cancer does it put first?

choices.label: Carcinoma cervix, as the old PYQ key says
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Cervix is the answer old keys expected, so it feels safe. Its top place has since changed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the old key is doing the talking. Check current registry figures before you trust a key.

say.text: Ask which cancer current registry figures put first in women, not which one older keys listed first.
Yes. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women in India and worldwide.
Older keys named cervix, but breast has overtaken it, so the current answer is breast.
A 50-year-old woman has a firm breast lump. Before neoadjuvant chemotherapy starts, the pathologist must report invasive or in situ status, and the ER, PR and HER2 receptors.
Which sample do you send?

choices.label: Core needle biopsy of the mass
Fine needle aspiration cytology of the mass
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Cytology is quick, and it is the test old keys named for a lump. A cell sample may not show invasion or give receptor status.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the old key is the likely source. Ask what the pathologist must report before choosing the sample.

say.text: Ask which sample can show whether the cancer invades, and what its receptors are, not which is quickest to take.
Yes. A core needle (trucut) biopsy gives histology, separating invasive from in situ disease, and reports ER, PR and HER2.
Older keys expected FNAC for a lump; current practice uses core because of this histology.

A 52-year-old woman has a 3 cm tumour with peau d'orange (orange-peel skin) over it. The skin is neither red nor warm, and the breast is not swollen. One firm node sits above the collarbone on the same side.
Give the T, N and M categories together.

choices.label: T4b, M1, since the node is distant
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Orange-peel skin looks like the inflammatory picture, so T4d tempts. The sign alone does not make the disease inflammatory; the whole clinical picture does.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the sign is doing the work. Check the full picture before you name the T category.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A node above the collarbone looks like distant spread, which is the old-key reading. Current staging keeps same-side nodes inside the nodal ladder.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the old M1 key is likely the source. Place the node on the nodal ladder first.

say.text: Work out the T category from the skin first. Then ask whether the node above the collarbone is nodal or distant.
Yes. Peau d'orange with no redness or warmth is skin involvement, T4b, and the 3 cm size does not change that.
The same-side supraclavicular node is N3c, and with no distant disease the M category stays M0.
A surgeon's note reads: T4a, because the tumour is fixed to the pectoralis major.
Your examiner asks you to check the note. Which correction is right?

choices.label: Fixity to pectoralis alone is not T4a
Fixity to pectoralis major makes it T4a
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
The muscle the tumour touches feels like chest wall, so it seems to count. The T4a category is set by the chest-wall structures the tumour reaches.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the muscle is doing the work. Check which structures the T4a category names.

say.text: Check the T4a list: which structures does it name for the chest wall?
Yes. Fixity to the pectoralis major is tested by contracting it, but that alone is not chest-wall disease.
The ribs, intercostal muscles or serratus anterior must be involved before the tumour is T4a.
A 58-year-old has a mass in one breast. Her MRI also shows an area in the other breast.
Which histology is most often bilateral or multicentric?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
NST is the commonest type, so it feels like the default for any type question. Commonness does not decide which type spreads to both breasts.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so commonness is doing the work. Ask which type behaves differently, not which is most frequent.

say.text: Ask which type tends to grow in both breasts, not which type is most common.
Yes. Lobular carcinoma loses E-cadherin, so cells grow in single file, and it is more often bilateral and multicentric.
A family carries a BRCA mutation on chromosome 13q.
Your classmate names BRCA1, the best-known gene. Which gene do you name?

choices.label: BRCA1, the gene linked to men's breast cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
BRCA1 is the familiar gene, so it feels like the default for any locus. Each gene has its own chromosome arm, and the arm in the stem decides which gene it is.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the familiar gene is doing the work. Match the arm to the gene first.

say.text: That choice is not right.
BRCA1 is the best-known gene, so it is tempting for every question. Male breast cancer is tied to the other gene, and the arm in the stem still settles this case.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the best-known gene is doing the work. Check which phenotype the stem describes.

say.text: The stem gives a chromosome arm. Match the arm to the gene before you consider anything else.
Yes. BRCA2 lies on 13q, and it is the gene more associated with male breast cancer.
A 58-year-old has taken tamoxifen for three years for ER-positive cancer.
She now reports vaginal bleeding. What is your main concern?

choices.label: Tamoxifen protects the lining, so cancer is unlikely
Endometrial carcinoma, a recognised tamoxifen risk
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Tamoxifen blocks oestrogen in the breast, so it is easy to assume it protects the uterus too. It acts differently in the endometrium, so the bleeding needs checking.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the breast effect is being carried over. Ask what the drug does to the uterine lining.

say.text: Think about what tamoxifen does to the uterine lining, not only to the breast.
Yes. Tamoxifen raises the risk of endometrial carcinoma, so bleeding on it always needs evaluation.
Raloxifene does not carry that endometrial risk, which is why it can be used in chemoprevention.
A classmate writes: 'ER-positive, so give tamoxifen.' Your patient is 70, past menopause, with ER-positive early cancer.
Which correction do you give?

choices.label: Aromatase inhibitor, since she is postmenopausal
Tamoxifen, since ER positivity is the rule
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
ER positivity is the cue the classmate used, and it feels like it settles the drug. It leaves out her menopausal status, which changes the choice.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so one marker is doing the work. Check what the menopausal status changes.

say.text: ER positivity is only half the question. Ask what her menopausal status changes about where her oestrogen comes from.
Yes. After menopause, aromatase inhibitors are preferred; tamoxifen is the usual hormonal agent before menopause.
A 48-year-old has classic lobular carcinoma in situ, found by chance on a biopsy taken for another lesion. There is no invasive cancer.
What is the main decision for her?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
LCIS can look like cancer under the microscope, so removing the breast feels safe. It marks risk in both breasts rather than being an invasive cancer to remove.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the pathology look is doing the work. Ask what this lesion predicts.

say.text: Ask what LCIS predicts: is it a cancer to remove, or a marker of risk in both breasts?
Yes. Classic LCIS is managed with surveillance, and chemoprevention can be considered.
It is a risk marker in either breast, so the follow-up plan is what matters.
A 42-year-old has bloody discharge from a single duct. Nothing is palpable.
Her registrar asks for the most common cause, and for the cause you must still rule out. Which answer fits?

choices.label: Carcinoma breast is the most common cause
Intraductal papilloma is most common; carcinoma must still be excluded
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Carcinoma is the cause you most fear, so it feels like the commonest one too. Frequency and alarm are different questions; a sign can be dangerous without being common.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the alarm is answering a frequency question. Keep the two apart.

say.text: Separate two questions: which cause is most frequent, and which must never be missed.
Yes. Intraductal papilloma is the most common cause of bloody nipple discharge.
Bloody discharge is still a sign to exclude carcinoma, so it is not dismissed.
A trainee's viva answer is about two operations for an operable breast cancer.
Which statement correctly separates Halsted from MRM?

choices.label: Halsted is still the standard; MRM is the lesser operation
Halsted removes pectoralis major and minor; MRM keeps major
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Radical sounds like the most definitive operation, so the bigger one seems the standard. Current practice moved towards less extensive surgery.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the word radical is doing the work. Ask which operation current practice uses.

say.text: Look at which muscles each operation removes, then ask which one current practice uses.
Yes. Halsted removes the breast, pectoralis major and minor, and all axillary levels.
MRM removes the breast and axillary nodes but keeps pectoralis major.
A HER2-positive patient on trastuzumab asks whether her heart could be damaged the way it is with doxorubicin.
What do you tell her?

choices.label: Same as doxorubicin: dose-related, largely permanent
Usually reversible, and not tied to total dose
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That choice is not right.
Anthracyclines set the pattern for cardiotoxicity, so one rule seems to cover every breast drug. Trastuzumab's heart effect follows a different pattern.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the anthracycline pattern is doing the work. Ask which drug's effect builds up with dose.

say.text: Ask whether this drug's heart effect builds up with total dose like doxorubicin, or usually recovers.
Yes. Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is usually reversible and not dose-related.
Doxorubicin's cardiomyopathy is the dose-dependent, largely permanent one, so the two must not be merged.
